items.q: Solid lead bromide does not conduct electricity, but molten lead bromide does. Why?
items.correct: Melting frees the ions so they can move through the liquid
items.misconception: Melting changes the neutral atoms into charged ions
items.why: Ions are first met in the context of a reaction that forms them, so any change that makes conduction possible is read as the moment the ions are made. The ions exist in the solid compound already. Melting or dissolving does not create them; it only lets them move.
items.random_wrong: Melting releases electrons that then carry the charge

items.q: Which of these can act as an electrolyte?
items.correct: Sodium chloride dissolved in pure water
items.misconception: Sodium chloride kept as a dry white solid
items.why: Students learn that ionic compounds contain charged particles and assume charge alone is enough, without asking whether the charges can move. Conduction needs charges that are free to move. In the solid the ions are locked in fixed positions in the lattice; melting or dissolving frees them, which is why only the melt and the solution are electrolytes.
items.random_wrong: A copper wire carrying an electric current

items.q: During electrolysis, where do the positively charged ions move to?
items.correct: To the cathode, the negative electrode
items.misconception: To the positive electrode, which attracts them
items.why: Under pressure students match the words 'positive ion' to 'positive electrode' rather than applying the rule that opposite charges attract. Opposite charges attract, so positive ions move to the negative electrode and negative ions move to the positive electrode.
items.random_wrong: To the anode, which is the negative electrode

items.q: Ions are discharged at the electrodes during electrolysis. What is produced?
items.correct: Elements, as the ions lose their charge
items.misconception: New compounds that build up on each electrode
items.why: Most reactions students meet make compounds, so they expect a product more complicated than a single element. Discharge removes the charge from an ion, leaving neutral atoms that join to form an element: a metal or a non-metal, never a new compound.
items.random_wrong: The original compound, moved to the electrodes

items.q: Molten lead bromide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. What is produced at the cathode?
items.correct: Lead, the metal, collects at the cathode
items.misconception: Bromine, because the non-metals form there
items.why: Metals are strongly associated with positive things, so the metal is placed at the positive electrode without tracking the charge on its ion. The metal forms a positive ion, so it is attracted to the negative electrode (cathode); the non-metal ion is negative and goes to the anode.
items.random_wrong: Hydrogen, made from water in this melt

items.q: What is seen at the anode when molten lead bromide is electrolysed?
items.correct: Orange-brown bromine vapour is given off
items.misconception: A silvery bead of molten lead collects on it
items.why: Metals are strongly associated with positive things, so the metal is placed at the positive electrode without tracking the charge on its ion. The metal forms a positive ion, so it is attracted to the negative electrode (cathode); the non-metal ion is negative and goes to the anode.
items.random_wrong: Colourless oxygen gas bubbles away from it

items.q: Molten magnesium chloride is electrolysed. Which products are formed?
items.correct: Magnesium at the negative electrode and chlorine at the positive
items.misconception: Chlorine at the negative electrode, magnesium at the positive
items.why: Metals are strongly associated with positive things, so the metal is placed at the positive electrode without tracking the charge on its ion. The metal forms a positive ion, so it is attracted to the negative electrode (cathode); the non-metal ion is negative and goes to the anode.
items.random_wrong: Hydrogen at the negative electrode and chlorine at the positive

items.q: Molten aluminium oxide is electrolysed. Which products are formed?
items.correct: Aluminium at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
items.misconception: Hydrogen at the cathode, oxygen at the anode
items.why: The aqueous rules are learned as facts about electrolysis in general, and are then applied to a molten compound where no water is present. Hydrogen and hydroxide ions come from water. A molten compound contains no water, so the products can only be the two elements in the compound.
items.random_wrong: Oxygen at the cathode with aluminium at the anode

items.q: Why is aluminium extracted by electrolysis rather than by reduction with carbon?
items.correct: Aluminium is too reactive to be reduced by carbon
items.misconception: Electrolysis is the cheaper of the two methods
items.why: Students assume industry always picks the cheapest route, so the method actually used must be the cheap one. Electrolysis is expensive, using large amounts of energy to melt the compound and produce the current. It is used only when carbon cannot do the job.
items.random_wrong: Carbon needs a higher temperature than the furnace reaches

items.q: Why does extracting a metal by electrolysis use so much energy?
items.correct: Energy is needed to melt the compound and produce the current
items.misconception: The ore must first be purified using costly chemicals
items.why: Students know extraction is expensive and attach the cost to the stage they can picture most easily. The specification is specific: large amounts of energy are used to melt the compounds and to produce the electrical current.
items.random_wrong: Electrolysis needs far more ore than reduction by carbon

items.q: In the manufacture of aluminium, what is the electrolyte and what is the positive electrode made of?
items.correct: A molten mixture of aluminium oxide and cryolite, carbon anode
items.misconception: Aluminium oxide dissolved in warm water, with a steel anode
items.why: Most electrolysis the student has seen in class uses solutions, so a solution is assumed here too. Aluminium oxide is insoluble, and water would give hydrogen at the cathode instead of aluminium. The electrolyte is a molten mixture of aluminium oxide and cryolite.
items.random_wrong: Molten cryolite on its own, with an anode made of carbon

items.q: Why is cryolite mixed with the aluminium oxide?
items.correct: It lowers the melting point, so less energy is needed
items.misconception: It acts as a catalyst and speeds the process up
items.why: 'Something added that makes the process work better' is filed under catalyst, the only such idea many students have. Cryolite is not a catalyst. Aluminium oxide melts at over 2000 °C; the mixture with cryolite melts at a much lower temperature, saving energy.
items.random_wrong: It supplies all the aluminium ions that are discharged

items.q: Why must the positive electrode in the aluminium cell be replaced continually?
items.correct: Oxygen made there reacts with the carbon and wears it away
items.misconception: The heat of the molten mixture slowly melts the carbon
items.why: Wearing away is explained by the most obvious feature of the cell, its high temperature, rather than by a chemical reaction. Carbon does not melt at the temperature of the cell. Oxygen is discharged at the anode and reacts with the hot carbon to form carbon dioxide, so the electrode is eaten away.
items.random_wrong: The carbon dissolves in the melt because it is positive

items.q: When an aqueous solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes, what decides which ions are discharged?
items.correct: The relative reactivity of the elements involved
items.misconception: The size of the charge carried by each of the ions
items.why: Charge is the property students use to work out which electrode an ion moves to, so it is reused for the next decision as well. Charge decides which electrode an ion travels to. Which of the ions arriving there is actually discharged depends on the relative reactivity of the elements involved.
items.random_wrong: The mass of each of the ions present in the solution

items.q: Copper chloride solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the cathode?
items.correct: Copper, as it is less reactive than hydrogen
items.misconception: Hydrogen, because copper is less reactive than it
items.why: The rule is memorised as a pair of words without a reason, so the comparison is easily reversed under exam pressure. The less reactive element is the one discharged. If the metal is more reactive than hydrogen it stays in solution and hydrogen is produced.
items.random_wrong: Chlorine, since chloride ions are drawn there

items.q: Sodium sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the cathode?
items.correct: Hydrogen, as sodium is more reactive than hydrogen
items.misconception: Sodium, because it is the metal in the compound used
items.why: The molten-state rule 'metal at the cathode' is carried over to solutions, where water also supplies ions. In solution the cathode product depends on relative reactivity: a metal less reactive than hydrogen is produced, but if the metal is more reactive, hydrogen is produced instead.
items.random_wrong: Sulfur, which forms from the sulfate ions in solution

items.q: Sodium chloride solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the anode?
items.correct: Chlorine, as the solution holds halide ions
items.misconception: Sodium, which is drawn to the positive electrode
items.why: Under pressure students match the words 'positive ion' to 'positive electrode' rather than applying the rule that opposite charges attract. Opposite charges attract, so positive ions move to the negative electrode and negative ions move to the positive electrode.
items.random_wrong: Hydrogen, coming from the water in the solution

items.q: Copper sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the anode?
items.correct: Oxygen, as no halide ions are present
items.misconception: Sulfur dioxide, made from the sulfate ions
items.why: Students split the compound name in two and expect both halves to appear, without checking whether the ion is a halide. Only halide ions are discharged in place of hydroxide. With sulfate, nitrate or a similar ion, oxygen is produced at the anode from hydroxide ions.
items.random_wrong: Copper, plating onto the positive electrode

items.q: In the electrolysis of an aqueous solution, where do the hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions come from?
items.correct: From water molecules that break down in the solution
items.misconception: From the dissolved compound splitting into its ions
items.why: Students track only the compound they added and forget that water itself supplies ions. In the aqueous solution water molecules break down producing hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions; these are the extra ions available for discharge.
items.random_wrong: From hydrogen and oxygen gas dissolved in water

items.q: A student plans Required practical 3 and writes an idea down before starting. Which statement is a hypothesis the investigation could test?
items.correct: Solutions of halides will give a halogen at the anode
items.misconception: Copper chloride solution is a clear blue liquid
items.why: Hypothesis, observation and conclusion are all written in the same practical account, so the words blur together. A hypothesis is a testable idea put forward before the experiment, predicting what will happen and why. An observation is what is recorded during it.
items.random_wrong: Bubbles appeared at the negative electrode

items.q: In Required practical 3, the gas collected at the cathode gave a squeaky pop with a lit splint. What does this show?
items.correct: Hydrogen formed, so the metal is more reactive
items.misconception: Oxygen formed, because oxygen relights the splint
items.why: The two gas tests are learned together and the splint is the memorable part, so which splint goes with which gas gets swapped. Hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lit splint; oxygen relights a glowing splint; chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper.
items.random_wrong: Chlorine formed, since it bleaches damp litmus paper

items.q: At the cathode, positively charged ions gain electrons. How is this reaction described?
items.correct: Reduction, because electrons are gained
items.misconception: Oxidation, because the electrons are gained
items.why: The word reduction suggests something being made smaller, which fits losing a particle better than gaining one. Oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain of electrons. At the cathode positive ions gain electrons, so cathode reactions are reductions.
items.random_wrong: Oxidation, as the cathode is negative

items.q: At the anode, negatively charged ions lose electrons. How is this reaction described?
items.correct: Oxidation, as electrons are lost by the ions
items.misconception: Reduction, because electrons are lost
items.why: The word reduction suggests something being made smaller, which fits losing a particle better than gaining one. Oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain of electrons. At the cathode positive ions gain electrons, so cathode reactions are reductions.
items.random_wrong: Reduction, since the anode is positive

items.q: Which pair of half equations represents the reactions at the two electrodes correctly?
items.correct: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ at the cathode, and 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ at the anode
items.misconception: 2H⁺ → H₂ + 2e⁻ at the cathode and 4OH⁻ + 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O at the anode
items.why: The half equation is copied as a pattern rather than read as electrons being supplied to, or taken from, the ion. At the cathode electrons are gained, so they appear with the reactants: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. At the anode they are lost, so they appear with the products.
items.random_wrong: H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂ at the cathode and OH⁻ → O₂ + H₂O + e⁻ at the anode

items.q: Which half equation shows hydrogen being produced at the cathode?
items.correct: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
items.why: Balancing is taught first with ordinary equations, where only atoms are counted, so the charges are not checked. The number of electrons must make the total charge the same on each side, as well as the atoms balancing. H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂ balances for charge (zero on each side) but not for atoms, so it is still wrong; 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ passes both tests.
items.random_wrong: 2H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂

items.q: Which half equation shows hydroxide ions being discharged at the anode?
items.correct: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻
items.misconception: 4OH⁻ → 2O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻
items.why: Balancing is taught first with ordinary equations, where only atoms are counted, so the charges are not checked. The number of electrons must make the total charge the same on each side, as well as the atoms balancing. H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂ balances for charge (zero on each side) but not for atoms, so it is still wrong; 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ passes both tests.
items.random_wrong: 2OH⁻ + 2e⁻ → O₂ + H₂O

items.q: The anode reaction may be written as 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ or as 4OH⁻ – 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O. How are the two related?
items.correct: They are the same reaction, written in two ways
items.misconception: The second one supplies electrons instead of removing them
items.why: Students read the equation as arithmetic on one line and take any term on the left as a reactant being supplied. 4OH⁻ – 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O and 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ say the same thing: the hydroxide ions lose four electrons.
items.random_wrong: The first is the anode one, the second the cathode one

items.q: Complete and balance the half equation for the reaction at the cathode in the aluminium cell.
items.correct: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al
items.misconception: 3Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → 3Al
items.why: Students look for a number in the formula to copy, and use a subscript or the number of ions instead of the size of the charge. The charge on the ion sets the number of electrons: Al³⁺ carries three positive charges, so Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al.
items.random_wrong: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → 3Al

items.q: Molten lead bromide is electrolysed. Which half equation shows the reaction at the cathode?
items.correct: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb
items.misconception: Pb²⁺ + e⁻ → Pb
items.why: Balancing is taught first with ordinary equations, where only atoms are counted, so the charges are not checked. The number of electrons must make the total charge the same on each side, as well as the atoms balancing. H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂ balances for charge (zero on each side) but not for atoms, so it is still wrong; 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ passes both tests.
items.random_wrong: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻

items.q: Sodium chloride solution is electrolysed. Which half equation shows the reaction at the anode?
items.correct: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
items.misconception: 2Cl⁻ + 2e⁻ → Cl₂
items.why: The half equation is copied as a pattern rather than read as electrons being supplied to, or taken from, the ion. At the cathode electrons are gained, so they appear with the reactants: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. At the anode they are lost, so they appear with the products.
items.random_wrong: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 4e⁻

items.q: What carries the current through molten lead bromide?
items.correct: Moving ions.
items.misconception: Electrons flow through the liquid, as they do through a wire.
items.why: The circuit outside the cell does carry electrons, and students extend that single picture to the liquid inside the cell. In the external circuit electrons flow; in the electrolyte the current is carried by ions moving to the electrodes, where electrons are transferred.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which electrode is the cathode?
items.correct: The negative one.
items.misconception: The cathode is positive and the anode is negative.
items.why: The two unfamiliar words are learned as a pair without an anchor, so the labels are attached to the wrong signs. Cathode means the negative electrode, which attracts positive ions; anode means the positive electrode, which attracts negative ions.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is Br⁻ the product at the anode?
items.correct: No. Bromine, Br₂, is the product.
items.misconception: The ion itself is given off at the electrode.
items.why: Students name the particle they know is attracted to the electrode and stop there, missing the electron transfer that discharges it. At the electrode the ion is discharged: bromide ions lose electrons and form bromine molecules, an element with no charge.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Could carbon extract aluminium if the furnace were hotter?
items.correct: No. Reactivity, not temperature, is what decides.
items.misconception: Any metal can be extracted with carbon if it is heated enough.
items.why: Heat is seen as a way of forcing any reaction to happen, so the reactivity order is treated as something temperature can overcome. Carbon can only remove oxygen from the oxide of a metal less reactive than carbon. Aluminium is more reactive, so it must be extracted by electrolysis.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where does the aluminium come from?
items.correct: From the aluminium oxide.
items.misconception: Cryolite supplies the aluminium ions that are discharged.
items.why: Cryolite is named in the same sentence as the aluminium and is assumed to be the source of the metal. The aluminium comes from the aluminium oxide. The cryolite is there to lower the melting point of the mixture.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the anode dissolve in the electrolyte?
items.correct: No. It reacts with the oxygen produced on it.
items.misconception: The positive electrode dissolves away because it is positive.
items.why: Electroplating and copper purification, where a metal anode really does dissolve, are half-remembered and applied to an inert carbon anode. An inert electrode does not dissolve. The carbon anode is lost because oxygen discharged on it burns it away as carbon dioxide.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is oxygen always the anode product in solution?
items.correct: No. A halide solution gives the halogen instead.
items.misconception: Oxygen is produced at the anode whatever the solution contains.
items.why: The 'water gives oxygen' half of the rule is remembered and the halide exception is dropped. Oxygen is produced at the anode unless the solution contains halide ions, in which case the halogen - chlorine, bromine or iodine - is produced.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does water break down into hydrogen and oxygen molecules in the solution?
items.correct: No. It produces hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions.
items.misconception: Water in the solution splits straight into H₂ and O₂.
items.why: The overall result of electrolysing dilute acid is remembered as 'water splits into hydrogen and oxygen', and that summary replaces the ion step. Water molecules break down producing hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions. The gases appear only after those ions are discharged at the electrodes.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why are graphite electrodes used in Required practical 3?
items.correct: Because they conduct and take no part in the reactions.
items.misconception: Any material that conducts will do as an electrode.
items.why: The electrode is thought of only as a way of getting current into the liquid, not as a possible reactant. The electrode must be inert as well as conducting. A reactive electrode would take part in the reaction and change the products being investigated.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the sign of the electrode tell you whether it is oxidation?
items.correct: No. What matters is whether electrons are lost or gained by the ions.
items.misconception: The positive electrode must be where reduction happens.
items.why: 'Positive' is matched with 'gain' and 'negative' with 'loss', so the sign of the electrode is used instead of the electron transfer. At the anode (positive) negative ions lose electrons, so it is oxidation. At the cathode (negative) positive ions gain electrons, so it is reduction.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is discharging an ion the same as neutralisation?
items.correct: No. It is a transfer of electrons, described as oxidation or reduction.
items.misconception: An ion losing its charge at an electrode is neutralisation.
items.why: Neutralisation is the only process students have met in which charge disappears, so the word is reused for discharge. Neutralisation is the reaction of an acid with a base. At an electrode the ion gains or loses electrons: gain of electrons is reduction, loss of electrons is oxidation.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is 'which gas forms at the cathode?' a hypothesis?
items.correct: No, it is a question the investigation asks.
items.misconception: A hypothesis is the question you are trying to answer.
items.why: Investigations start from a question, so the question is taken to be the hypothesis itself. The question sets the aim; the hypothesis is the answer you propose in advance, stated so that results can support or disprove it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
